title: SaaS Pricing Drift Report 2026: How to Verify Published Prices
description: A practical guide to finding stale SaaS prices, documenting vendor evidence, and comparing plan costs without relying on unsupported claims.
keyFindings: Pricing details can become stale when vendors rename plans, change limits, alter billing terms, or discontinue tiers.
A pricing discrepancy should be counted only when the published claim, current vendor source, date checked, and relevant plan are documented.
Small per-seat differences can materially change total cost for large teams, so compare the same seat count and billing period.
A price claim without a current source should be marked unverified rather than repeated as fact.
A reliable pricing audit needs a reproducible sample, transparent inclusion rules, source links, and dated evidence.

sections.title: Why pricing drift matters
sections.body: Buyers often rely on comparison pages when shortlisting software. If a page shows a discontinued plan, misses a new tier, or confuses monthly and annual billing, the shortlist and budget can be wrong. The risk is larger when prices vary by seat count, region, usage, or contract length.

sections.title: Evidence standard for this report
sections.body: A defensible discrepancy requires two preserved records: the exact third-party claim and the current official vendor source checked on a stated date. The comparison must use the same product, plan, currency, region, billing interval, and unit. Historical notes without a retrievable source are leads for further checking, not independently verified findings. This report does not present previously recorded discrepancy counts or individual price changes as confirmed until that evidence is available.

sections.title: Common patterns to investigate
sections.body: The following are audit patterns to check, not claims that a particular vendor currently has a specific price error.
items: A discontinued plan is still presented as available to new customers
A new entry tier is missing from an older comparison
Annual-billing prices are presented as monthly prices without explanation
Per-seat pricing is compared with flat-rate pricing
Feature availability is attributed to the wrong plan
A regional price or currency is presented as universal
Usage caps, minimum seats, or mandatory add-ons are omitted

sections.title: How to run a pricing verification
sections.body: Open the official pricing page and the third-party page. Capture the URL, date, plan name, currency, region, billing term, unit, minimum commitment, and limits. If the official page does not disclose the price, request an itemized quote or mark the price as quote-based. Do not infer a number from snippets or another aggregator.
items: Record the third-party claim verbatim and link to it
Capture the official vendor source and date checked
Confirm plan, region, currency and billing period match
Calculate the difference using the same unit
Keep screenshots or archived evidence where permitted
Update every internal page that repeats the claim

sections.title: Calculate the buyer impact
sections.body: Convert both prices to the same basis. For per-seat pricing, multiply the difference by the actual seat count and billing periods. Include required add-ons and usage overages separately. State the assumptions so readers can reproduce the calculation. Do not extrapolate one customer's quote to all customers.

sections.title: Limitations and updates
sections.body: SaaS prices change frequently and can be personalized by region, contract, or negotiation. A single observation does not establish an industry-wide pattern. Any future quantitative findings should include the sample, date window, source links, exclusions, and calculation method. Until those records are published, this page is a verification framework rather than a claim that a specific number of vendors is currently mispriced.

methodology: Pricing drift should be measured from dated, source-linked comparisons of third-party claims against official vendor pricing. This page intentionally avoids publishing specific discrepancy counts or current prices that cannot be substantiated from the available source trail.
